extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic theory and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative criteria and evaluative standards for assessing democratic governments (their laws, institutions, and social consequences), as discussed in a classical political-theory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular origin increases authority of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: “This popular origin...contributes prodigiously to increase its power. There is an amazing strength in the expression of the determination of a whole people, and when it declares itself the imagination of those who are most inclined to contest it is overawed by its authority.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether laws derive visibly from popular will; note that popular origin can augment obedience even if it reduces legislative wisdom. Parties therefore strive to create apparent majorities; the ability of laws to command obedience is increased when seen as the expression of the people's determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal stake of citizens in enforcing the law
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the United States everyone is personally interested in enforcing the obedience of the whole community to the law; for as the minority may shortly rally the majority to its principles, it is interested in professing that respect for the decrees of the legislator which it may soon have occasion to claim for its own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether citizens treat laws as self-imposed contracts and whether minorities have incentives to outwardly respect laws they might later change. This individual stake strengthens compliance and social enforcement of legal norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of the elective franchise and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the United States, except slaves, servants, and paupers in the receipt of relief...there is no class of persons who do not exercise the elective franchise, and who do not indirectly contribute to make the laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure inclusiveness of electoral participation; wider participation tends to increase legitimacy and obedience, though exclusions (legal or de facto) can undermine equality and protection of minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment or 'parental affection' for the law among classes
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is impossible...not to perceive that all classes display the utmost reliance upon the legislation of their country, and that they are attached to it by a kind of parental affection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cultural attitudes toward law: whether citizens view laws with trust and affection. Note exceptions (the wealthy may distrust laws in democracies) and how social position shapes legal attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pervasive political activity and civic engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cares of political life engross a most prominent place in the occupation of a citizen in the United States...This feeling pervades the most trifling habits of life; even the women frequently attend public meetings and listen to political harangues...Debating clubs are to a certain extent a substitute for theatrical entertainments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how widely political discussion, meetings, societies, and local deliberation penetrate everyday life. High civic activity broadens citizens' ideas, fosters self-respect, and trains them in public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's effect on economic/commercial activity
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have no doubt that the democratic institutions of the United States, joined to the physical constitution of the country, are the cause...of the prodigious commercial activity of the inhabitants. It is not engendered by the laws, but the people learns how to promote it by the experience derived from legislation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether democratic participation and legislative experience indirectly stimulate commerce and innovation; look for empirical signs of commercial dynamism linked to broad civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy produces many undertakings but less methodical execution
rubrics_metrics.description: “Democratic liberty is far from accomplishing all the projects it undertakes, with the skill of an adroit despotism. It frequently abandons them before they have borne their fruits...but in the end it produces more than any absolute government, and if it do fewer things well, it does a greater number of things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh quantity versus quality: democracies may initiate numerous reforms and projects but often lack perseverance or technical consistency. Evaluate persistence and follow-through of public projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutability/instability of laws and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mutability of the laws is an evil inherent in democratic government...In America the authority exercised by the legislative bodies is supreme...America is, at the present day, the country in the world where laws last the shortest time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine frequency of constitutional amendments, legislative turnover, and short legislative terms. High mutability indicates instability and caprice; compare archival records and amendment histories for measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and institutional mechanisms that amplify majority power
rubrics_metrics.description: “The legislature is, of all political institutions, the one which is most easily swayed by the wishes of the majority...the members of the legislature should be elected by the people immediately, and for a very brief term, in order to subject them...to the daily passion, of their constituents. ...elective judiciary; representatives pledged to a line of conduct.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify legal designs (direct, frequent elections; short terms; elective judges; pledged delegates) that make legislatures and officials highly responsive to majority passions. Such mechanisms increase majority dominance and reduce independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral authority and presumed infallibility of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: “The moral authority of the majority is partly based upon the notion that there is more intelligence and more wisdom in a great number of men collected together than in a single individual...The theory of equality is in fact applied to the intellect of man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for cultural or institutional beliefs that valorize majority wisdom over minority expertise. Such beliefs can legitimize majoritarian decisions and suppress dissent; consider how time and custom cement this authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of 'tyranny of the majority' and the need for transcendent justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “I hold it to be an impious and an execrable maxim that, politically speaking, a people has a right to do whatsoever it pleases...A general law—which bears the name of Justice—has been made and sanctioned, not only by a majority of this or that people, but by a majority of mankind. The rights of every people are consequently confined within the limits of what is just.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether majority decisions are constrained by higher principles of justice and universal rights. Systems should provide avenues of appeal beyond popular sovereignty (e.g., natural law, constitutional limits) to protect minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of institutional checks: independent branches and safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: “If, on the other hand, a legislative power could be so constituted as to represent the majority without necessarily being the slave of its passions; an executive, so as to retain a certain degree of uncontrolled authority; and a judiciary, so as to remain independent of the two other powers...a government would be formed which would still be democratic without incurring any risk of tyrannical abuse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess separation of powers, tenure and independence of judiciary, executive autonomy, and insulating mechanisms that prevent the legislature from being the mere instrument of transient majority passions. Lack of such checks invites majoritarian tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between tyranny and arbitrary power and implications for officers
rubrics_metrics.description: “A distinction must be drawn between tyranny and arbitrary power. Tyranny may be exercised by means of the law, and in that case it is not arbitrary; arbitrary power may be exercised for the good of the community at large, in which case it is not tyrannical.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public officials, distinguish lawful but oppressive majoritarian rule (tyranny) from discretionary actions by officers (arbitrariness). Scrutinize legal structures and the scope of discretionary authority to judge accountability and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority's control over officers fosters arbitrary administration
rubrics_metrics.description: “The majority has an entire control over the law when it is made and when it is executed; and as it possesses an equal authority over those who are in power and the community at large, it considers public officers as its passive agents, and readily confides the task of serving its designs to their vigilance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether public officers act as independent implementers of law or as passive instruments of majority will. Look for signs of politicized administration, lack of professional insulation, and susceptibility to majoritarian whims.
